rationale: Mixed-methods study examining adolescent girls' experiences of menstruation in rural schools of the Colombian Pacific (menarche information, pain, sociocultural taboos, absorbent materials, and poor access to school restrooms and water). Although institutional officers including the Vice-ministry of Water and Sanitation were interviewed regarding broad public policy neglect of menstrual inequality, the study investigates sociocultural menstrual constructs and school menstrual hygiene rather than any legal, administrative, regulatory, tenure, or tariff rule governing household or community water or sanitation service access (E03).
plain_vs_narrow_note: Under the narrow rule-type Criterion 2 reading, the study clearly excludes (E03) because it examines sociocultural constructs around menstruation and school menstrual hygiene conditions rather than any legal, regulatory, tenure, tariff, or administrative rule governing water or sanitation service access. Under the literal plain Criterion 2 wording covering any institutional or governance factor, it would be marked unsure because institutional officers from the Vice-ministry of Water and Sanitation and public policy management gaps were included in the qualitative inquiry alongside school restroom and water access.

evidence_quotes.quote: This study showed that insufficient information at the time of menarche, pain, poor access to restrooms, water and absorbent materials, as well as existing prejudices, cause menstruation to be experienced with pain and concealment.

Social and cultural constructs around menstruation in the municipalities studied lead to its configuration as a negative experience, which generates and reinforces taboos that materialize in inequity, stigma and discrimination against girls.
institutional officers from the Municipal Health and Education Secretariats, the Ministries of Health and Education, and the Vice-ministry of Water and Sanitation.
